name: Pectoral implants

lead:
Pectoral implants are solid silicone implants shaped like the pectoralis major, placed through a small incision to give men a fuller, more defined chest. They are used by men who want more chest volume than training gives, by those with asymmetry or a sunken chest, and in reconstruction for conditions such as Poland syndrome.
Published experience is mostly surgeon case series, such as a 2008 report on 21 patients with custom-made implants who were satisfied with the results.

paras: The implant is selected or custom-made to match the person's chest dimensions and inserted by a plastic surgeon, typically under general anaesthesia, with a recovery period afterwards. Surgeons often pair it with treatment of gynecomastia where needed.

As with other implant surgery, risks include infection, bleeding, fluid collection, scarring, asymmetry, implant shifting or hardening, and need for revision. It is surgery under anaesthesia and should be assessed by a qualified plastic surgeon.

angle.text: The implant adds volume without relying on muscle growth. It is used by men with underdeveloped or asymmetrical chests and in reconstruction.

lead: Pectoral implants are soft, solid silicone implants designed to mimic the size and shape of the pectoralis major, placed to enhance or restore the male chest [1]. A 1991 review in Clinics in Plastic Surgery described implants developed in several sizes and shapes to match the muscle and nipple-areolar complex, with soft solid silicone of similar height, length and thickness to the muscle [1]. For looks, the implant adds chest volume and contour directly, without depending on muscle growth, so a man whose pecs are underdeveloped, asymmetrical or sunken can have a fuller, more defined chest.

They serve people seeking chest enhancement, those with muscular atrophy or injury, and patients with congenital chest differences; an Aesthetic Plastic Surgery series of 21 patients used manufactured, custom-made implants in three groups: 18 seeking enhancement, one with muscle atrophy and two with muscle injuries [2]. The authors reported satisfying results [2]. Custom silicone implants are also a first-line reconstruction for Poland syndrome, in which the pectoralis muscle is partly or completely absent, and are used for some cases of pectus excavatum (sunken chest) [3][4].

As a cosmetic operation for men with otherwise normal chests, the procedure dates to 1988 and has stayed uncommon: reported US totals were 32 in 1994 and a few hundred a year in the 2010s, well below male breast reduction [5]. It is discussed on bodybuilding forum T Nation, where members have commented on a perceived increase in men getting silicone pectoral implants and on their opinions of the operation [6][7].
infobox: Solid silicone, soft solid rather than gel-filled [1]
Men seeking chest enhancement; atrophy, injury, congenital difference [2]

paras: Implants are produced in a range of sizes and shapes to follow the pectoralis major, and are soft solid silicone rather than gel-filled [1]. The 1991 review also noted improved gynecomastia techniques, including liposuction with circum-areolar excision, helping surgeons obtain a smooth, flat chest [1]. A 2002 paper in Aesthetic Plastic Surgery described pairing anatomical pectoral implants with liposculpture as a concept in male chest reshaping [8].

Implants can be selected from manufactured sizes or custom-made from a patient's chest dimensions, and in reconstructive work a three-dimensional reconstruction from a scan guides a computer-designed medical silicone implant [2][3][4]. A Toronto plastic surgeon told Vice in 2018 that he recommends a patient-specific, custom-made implant for chest concerns, and that calf and pec implants are typically silicone and firmer than breast implants [9]. Coverage describes placement through an incision in the armpit, and Poland syndrome descriptions give an incision of about 8 cm under general anaesthesia [3][5].

Cosmetic enhancement: men who train but are dissatisfied with chest development, or who want size they have not built, are the group most associated with the procedure; Mel magazine reports that by the late 1990s the typical patient was an amateur bodybuilder in this position [5]. The Toronto surgeon said patients often arrive with social media photos and cited concern about a caved-in area in the middle of the chest [9].

Asymmetry and congenital difference: Poland syndrome is a birth difference in which the pectoralis muscle is partly or completely absent, usually on one side, estimated at about 1 in 20,000 births with males affected more often than females; custom silicone implants are described as the first-line reconstruction, though the implant is primarily cosmetic and does not restore strength [3]. A 2024 paper in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery Global Open describes a surgical algorithm for Poland syndrome based on thorax, breast and nipple-areola classification [10].

Sunken chest: pectus excavatum affects an estimated 1 in 150 to 1 in 1,000 births, males about three times as often as females; among the options, custom silicone implants placed beneath the muscle correct the appearance but do not address heart or lung problems, unlike the Nuss bar procedure first performed in 1987 [4].

Gynecomastia: enlarged male breast tissue affects about 35 percent of men and up to 70 percent of adolescent boys to some degree; surgery is considered when it persists beyond 12 months or causes distress, and the 1991 review treated chest correction and gynecomastia together [1][11].

According to a history in Mel magazine, methods were first developed in the 1970s to help people with Poland syndrome, and in 1988 Mel Bircoll, chief of plastic surgery at Beverly Hills Medical Center, pioneered a version for men with otherwise normal pectoral development; the first implant was about 7 by 3 by 1 inches and was inserted through armpit incisions [5]. Poland syndrome itself was named in 1962 by plastic surgeon Patrick Clarkson after Alfred Poland, who described a related deformity in 1841 [3].

In September 1990, US Magazine reported the implants were available to the public for $6,500, one surgeon predicted they would become as popular among men as breast augmentation was among women, and Newsweek reported that men made up nearly 20 percent of plastic surgery patients, up from 5 percent in the early 1980s [5]. The procedure was nicknamed after Arnold Schwarzenegger, according to the same account [5].

Demand stayed small. By 1991 Bircoll had performed about 50 operations in 18 months, only 32 pectoral implants were performed on men in 1994, and USA Today called it a fringe procedure in 2004 when 206 operations were reported the previous year; procedures rose 43 percent from 2011 to 2012 to 317, still far below roughly 20,000 male breast reductions that year [5]. A plastic surgeon quoted in 2014 said most men were not interested in a cosmetic procedure that adds no muscle mass or strength [5].

In 2018 a Toronto surgeon told Vice that his own volume was about 25 to 40 pectoral implant procedures a year and that interest in male cosmetic surgery had risen sharply with social media; he cited American Society of Plastic Surgeons figures of more than 1.3 million cosmetic procedures on US men in 2017 [9].

In T Nation threads from 2002 and 2008, members reacted to male pectoral implants; one 2002 poster called them equally unwise as breast implants, and a 2008 poster pointed to a news report that silicone pectoral implants were on the rise [6][7]. A 2005 thread from a lifter with a jutting sternum compared his chest with post-operative pictures from corrective surgery and wondered about options [12], and a 2006 thread joked about replacing lifting with implants [13]. These are individual opinions, not survey data.

Compared with training, pectoral implants occupy a distinct place in physique discussion: bodybuilding forums emphasise muscle built through lifting, while implants supply shape and volume at the cost of surgery. Mel magazine notes that surgeons in the early 1990s, some in Florida, declined to perform the operation and pointed to diet and exercise as alternatives [5].

As with other implant surgery, risks listed in surgical sources include infection, bleeding, fluid collection, scarring, asymmetry, implant shifting, numbness and revision. Case literature describes late problems: a 2021 case report in Medicine described a 44-year-old man whose custom silicone chest implant, placed 14 years earlier for Poland syndrome, developed a large delayed fluid collection with implant perforations and a thick capsule; cytology excluded implant-associated lymphoma, the implant and capsule were removed, and he had no recurrence at one year [14]. The authors concluded that long-term follow-up and patient education are needed [14].

Mel magazine reports a 1999 case in which a bodybuilder was left with breast implants after an unlicensed practitioner operated on him, and that reports in 2012 said industrial silicone from the Poly Implant Prothese scandal had also been used in pectoral implants [5]. Gynecomastia surgery, often combined with chest work, has its own listed complications including hematoma, infection, asymmetry and altered sensation [11].

Evidence is limited to surgical series. A 2008 Aesthetic Plastic Surgery report of 21 patients using custom-made pectoral implants described technique and reported satisfying results, including enhancement of the chest [2]. A 1991 review covers implant design and gynecomastia correction [1]. A 2002 paper discusses combining anatomical pectoral implants with liposculpture [8]. A 2024 paper on Poland syndrome describes surgical algorithms for chest-wall reconstruction [10], and a 2021 case report documents a late seroma after a custom implant [14].

lore.intro: Pectoral implants are mentioned on bodybuilding forums as an alternative to training or as a topic of debate [6][7][13].
